chunks: Ali ibn Ibrahim, from his father, from Al-Nawfali, from Al-Sakuni, from Ja'far, from his father, from Ali (peace be upon him), that he was asked

about a tree, the root of which is in the Haram (sanctuary) and its branches are in the Hil (unrestricted area). A bird was on one of its branches; a man threw [a stone] at it and felled it. He (peace be upon him) said: 'Upon him is its compensation, when its root is in the Haram.'
ai.seo_question: What is the ruling on hunting a bird from a tree whose root is in the Haram but branches are outside?
ai.summary: This hadith from al-Kafi elucidates the principle of 'origin determines status' (asl al-shay') in Shia jurisprudence, ruling that the sanctity of the tree's root extends to its branches, thereby making the bird hunted from the branch liable for compensation. It highlights the precise spatial boundaries of Al-Haram and demonstrates how jurists apply logical deduction to complex physical scenarios involving shared boundaries. This ruling underscores the strict protection of wildlife within the sacred precincts, a key aspect of Hajj and Umrah rituals.
